problemText: Water sitting in an ocean is warmed by energy from the sun and changes into an invisible gas that rises into the air. What is the name of this stage of the water cycle?
choices: Collection
Condensation
Precipitation
Evaporation
hints: This stage happens first, when the sun's energy warms liquid water.
The word contains 'vapor,' and that gas is what forms during this stage.

problemText: A puddle on the playground disappears on a hot, dry afternoon without any person removing the water or the puddle draining away. Which stage of the water cycle is responsible for the puddle vanishing?
choices: Evaporation, because the sun's warmth changed the water into rising invisible vapor
Condensation, because cooling water vapor forms liquid droplets that cluster together in the air
Precipitation, because water is falling from clouds and landing on the ground as rain or snow
Collection, because liquid water is gathering and storing in oceans, lakes, and underground reserves
hints: Look for which stage involves the sun warming liquid water and turning it into a gas.
The puddle is disappearing into the air, not falling from the sky or gathering into a lake.

problemText: High in the sky, water vapor that has risen from the ocean cools as it reaches a higher altitude. The cooled water vapor changes back into countless tiny liquid droplets that cluster together and float in the air. Which stage of the water cycle is being described?
choices: Evaporation, because water is changing from a liquid into an invisible gas that rises into the atmosphere
Condensation, because water vapor is cooling and becoming liquid water droplets
Precipitation, because the liquid droplets have accumulated and are now heavy enough to fall as rain
Collection, because water droplets are merging together and flowing toward rivers and oceans
hints: This stage happens when something cools down and changes from a gas back into a liquid.
The tiny droplets floating together in the air form a cloud, which is the definition of this stage.

problemText: A student observes a lake early in the morning and notices the water level is slightly lower than it was the previous afternoon. Later that same day, a cloud forms above the lake, and by evening, rain falls and raises the lake's level back up. Place the correct stage name on each event: the water level dropping in the morning, the cloud forming during the afternoon, and the rain falling in the evening. Which choice lists all three stages in the correct order?
choices: Evaporation, precipitation, condensation
Condensation, evaporation, precipitation
Evaporation, condensation, precipitation
Precipitation, condensation, evaporation
hints: The water level dropped because warmth from the sun turned liquid water into rising vapor; that's where the cycle begins.
After vapor rises and the cloud forms, the droplets inside grow heavy and fall—which is the third stage, not the second.

problemText: A student claims: 'Once rain falls from a cloud onto the ground, that is the final stage and the water cycle is complete.' Is this claim correct or incorrect? Why or why not, in terms of the water cycle's four stages?
choices: The claim is correct because precipitation is the last stage, and once water reaches the ground the cycle stops.
The claim is incorrect because after precipitation, the water immediately evaporates back into the atmosphere, skipping any intermediate step between rainfall and the formation of new clouds.
The claim is incorrect because after precipitation, the water must undergo condensation again in order to form clouds and cycle back through the atmosphere rather than remaining on the ground.
The claim is incorrect because collection happens after precipitation, and collection returns water to lakes and oceans where evaporation can start the cycle again.
hints: Remember that the water cycle is a loop with no ending point—the fourth stage leads back to the first.
After rain falls (precipitation), water gathers into oceans, lakes, and rivers; that gathering is the stage that comes next.

problemText: A river flows into the ocean on the coast. A fish scientist tracks a single water droplet in that river as it enters the ocean and sits there for several weeks. Without external human interference, describe which four stages that droplet will move through next, in order, and explain why it returns to a location where the river cycle can begin again.
choices: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection—the water evaporates from the ocean, condenses into a cloud, falls as rain, and collects in a river or lake where it can flow back to the ocean.
Collection, precipitation, condensation, evaporation—the water collects in the ocean, falls as rain, condenses into a cloud, and evaporates back into the ocean without ever returning to the river.
Condensation, precipitation, evaporation, collection—the water condenses as it sits in the ocean, falls as rain above the land, evaporates into the sky, and collects in rivers.
Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, evaporation—the water evaporates from the ocean, condenses twice into clouds, and falls as rain, then immediately evaporates again with no collection step.
hints: The four stages must happen in the same order every time: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.
For the droplet to return to the river or a location where it can flow back to the ocean, it must be collected in a lake or river on land after it falls as precipitation.

problemText: Which of the following is a complete definition of an ecosystem? Use the lesson definition to pick the correct answer.
choices: Only the plants and animals that live in one location, excluding all nonliving components like soil and water
Every living and nonliving thing sharing one place, considered together
The largest animals that live in a particular area along with the vegetation they depend on for food
Only the water, soil, and rocks in one spot, separated from any organisms that might inhabit them
hints: Remember: an ecosystem includes BOTH living things AND nonliving things, not just one kind.
Think about whether the definition should mention everything in the place or just some parts.

problemText: A student observes a small pond and lists these parts: lily pads, algae, fish, water, mud, sunlight, and insects. Which of the following correctly separates the biotic parts from the abiotic parts?
choices: Biotic: water, mud, sunlight. Abiotic: lily pads, algae, fish, insects
Biotic: fish and insects. Abiotic: lily pads, algae, water, mud, sunlight
Biotic: lily pads, algae, fish, insects. Abiotic: water, mud, sunlight
Biotic: lily pads and algae. Abiotic: fish, insects, water, mud, sunlight
hints: Use the three-part test: does it grow, need energy to survive, and make more of its own kind?
Remember that plants pass all three tests, so they are biotic even though they do not move.

problemText: A student watches a beetle moving quickly across a log and says: 'The beetle must be living because it moves on its own.' Based on the lesson test for living things, what is the problem with this reasoning?
choices: The student only named one test instead of checking all three at once
Beetles do not actually move, so the student made a false observation
Something that moves is automatically nonliving, not living
Movement is not one of the three tests for determining if something is living
hints: The three tests are: does it grow, does it need energy to survive, and can it make more of its own kind.
Think about a plant—it can be living without moving at all.

problemText: An apple tree in an orchard grows in soil, receives sunlight, and produces apples that birds eat. A student says: 'The orchard is the apple tree's habitat because that is where it lives.' Explain what is wrong with this statement and identify what the orchard actually is.
choices: The statement is wrong because the habitat is a small, specific spot where one organism lives, not the entire place. The orchard is the ecosystem.
The statement is wrong because a habitat must be nonliving, and the orchard contains living things like birds. The orchard is the ecosystem.
The statement is wrong because an ecosystem cannot contain a habitat inside it. The apple tree itself is the habitat.
The statement is wrong because a habitat is larger than an ecosystem. The orchard is the habitat and the soil is the ecosystem.
hints: A habitat is always smaller than the ecosystem—it is one spot inside it where one particular organism lives.
The entire orchard with all its living and nonliving parts together is the ecosystem.

problemText: A student examines a forest ecosystem and identifies the following: oak trees, deer, soil, rain water, moss on tree trunks, air, insects living under bark, and fallen leaves. The student then claims: 'Since some living things are plants and some are animals, this forest must actually be two ecosystems, not one.' Why is this reasoning incorrect, and what term describes the smaller spots where individual organisms live?
choices: The reasoning is wrong because an ecosystem must contain both living and nonliving things in balance, and different types of organisms do not create separate ecosystems. The spots where individual organisms live are called biomes.

The reasoning is wrong because an ecosystem includes all living and nonliving things in one place, even when there are many different kinds of organisms. The specific spots where individual organisms live are called habitats.

The reasoning is wrong because ecosystems are defined by their location and all the organisms and nonliving features within that location, regardless of how many different types of plants and animals are present. The spots where organisms live are called zones.

The reasoning is wrong because the diversity of living things in one area actually strengthens the ecosystem rather than dividing it into separate parts. The spots where organisms live are called niches.
hints: An ecosystem is ONE place with BOTH living and nonliving parts together—even if there are many different types of living things.
The term for a small, specific spot inside an ecosystem where one particular organism lives comes directly from the vocabulary in the lesson.

problemText: A coastal tide pool contains sea stars, crabs, seaweed, salt water, smooth pebbles, and air above the water. A student creates a closed glass jar containing only seaweed, a small amount of water, and one pebble—a miniature copy of the tide pool. The student then claims: 'My jar is an ecosystem because it has some of the same living and nonliving parts as the tide pool.' Using the lesson definition of ecosystem and habitat, evaluate whether the jar meets the criteria to be called an ecosystem, and explain what would be missing.
choices: The jar is not a complete ecosystem because it lacks the variety of living organisms and the complex interactions between multiple types of plants, animals, and nonliving parts that define a real ecosystem like the tide pool.

The jar is not a complete ecosystem because the seaweed cannot obtain enough sunlight inside a glass container to produce food through photosynthesis, which would prevent it from functioning as a true ecosystem.

The jar is not a complete ecosystem because a single organism living alone in a space does not represent the living and nonliving parts sharing one place the way a real ecosystem does. A true ecosystem needs multiple types of living things interacting with the nonliving environment together.
The jar is not a complete ecosystem because the small amount of water and limited pebbles cannot provide enough nonliving resources to support the living organisms for an extended period of time.
hints: Think about what 'sharing one place' means in the ecosystem definition—does a jar with only one type of plant living in it match that description?

Compare the jar to the worked example of the pond: the pond had different kinds of organisms (plants, insects, frogs) all living together with the nonliving parts. Does the jar have that same kind of variety?

problemText: A meteorologist reports that it is raining and 22 degrees Celsius in the city of Greenfield right now. Is this statement about Greenfield's weather or its climate?
choices: Climate, because it describes the long-term average conditions that meteorologists record over many years.
Climate, because it tells you the temperature and precipitation for that location.
Weather, because it describes what the atmosphere is doing at one place right now.
Weather, because it reports conditions observed in the present moment rather than a pattern over time.
hints: Ask yourself: does this statement describe right now, or does it describe the pattern Greenfield usually has?
The key word in the statement is 'right now' — that tells you whether you are looking at a moment or a pattern.

problemText: Coastal City is known for having a warm, dry climate. Yesterday, Coastal City had one day of heavy rain and cooler temperatures. Does this one rainy day mean that Coastal City's climate is actually warm and wet, not warm and dry?
choices: No, because climate only includes the days that match the usual pattern.
Yes, because the actual conditions changed from warm and dry to cool and wet.
Yes, because climate must match every single day of weather that occurs there.
No, because one day of rain is weather, not a description of the climate pattern.
hints: Remember: a place can have one kind of climate and still have a day that does not match it.
Ask yourself whether one day, no matter how unusual, is enough to change how a place's climate is described.

problemText: A student wrote two statements about a place called Millbrook. Statement 1: 'It snowed in Millbrook last Tuesday.' Statement 2: 'Millbrook has a cold, snowy climate.' Can both statements be true at the same time? Explain why or why not.
choices: Yes, because the snow last Tuesday is weather, and the cold, snowy climate is the long-term pattern Millbrook usually has.
No, because one snow event means the place cannot be classified as having any consistent climate at all.
Yes, but only if temperatures in Millbrook drop below freezing on most days throughout the year.
No, because a single weather event that happened in the past cannot coexist with a climate description of the same place.
hints: Think about the difference between a single event and a repeated pattern.
Weather and climate answer two different questions about the very same place — neither one cancels the other out.

problemText: A weather forecaster says: 'Tomorrow in Plainville, it will be cold and icy, which is unusual for this time of year. Plainville's climate is usually warm and mild.' The forecaster is making two claims. Identify which claim is about weather and which is about climate, and explain why each one is classified that way.
choices: Cold and icy tomorrow is climate because unusual events define the overall pattern; warm and mild is weather because the word 'usually' indicates a short time frame.
Cold and icy tomorrow is weather because it names a short stretch of time; warm and mild climate is climate because it describes the pattern Plainville usually has year after year.
Both are climate because the forecaster is describing what Plainville's conditions will be like in the future.
Cold and icy tomorrow is weather because the forecaster noted it as unusual; warm and mild is climate because it represents the stable, predictable conditions.
hints: The key question to ask is: does each statement describe right now or a few days ahead, or does it describe the pattern a place is usually like?
One statement talks about tomorrow; the other talks about what is usual across time — that difference is what separates weather from climate.

problemText: A place called Drybrook had a very rainy month last year. The local newspaper wrote: 'Drybrook's climate may be changing to wet and rainy.' Is this conclusion correct? Why or why not, based on what climate means?
choices: No, because climate describes only temperature measurements, and rainfall data cannot be used to define climate.
Yes, because Drybrook actually received significant rain, which shows the climate pattern has shifted permanently.
No, because one rainy month is weather, not enough evidence of a climate pattern that repeats year after year.
Yes, because the newspaper observed real rainfall data from Drybrook, proving the climate definition has been met.
hints: To describe a climate, you need to know what kind of weather a place has over many years, not just what happened during one month.
A climate is a pattern that repeats year after year — can one rainy month show that kind of long-term pattern?

problemText: A student is studying three places: Alpine Town in mountains where it snows most winters; Desert City in the lowlands where it almost never rains; and Bayshore Village on the coast where ocean winds are common. A spring weather report shows: Alpine Town had no snow for two weeks, Desert City had a brief rainstorm yesterday, and Bayshore Village had completely calm air for three days. For each place, the student needs to decide whether this spring report is evidence that the place's climate has changed. What should the student conclude, and why?
choices: Only Desert City shows climate change, because deserts are defined by permanent dryness while mountains and coasts are places where weather can shift unpredictably from day to day.
All three reports show climate change, because each place's actual weather in spring differs from what the student has learned about its typical conditions and expected seasonal patterns.

Alpine Town and Desert City show climate change, but Bayshore Village does not, because atmospheric wind patterns are more stable than precipitation patterns and can recover quickly from disturbances.
None of these weather reports are evidence of climate change, because each describes a few days or one recent event, not a pattern repeated year after year, which is what climate is.
hints: To know whether climate has changed, you would need to know whether the pattern of weather has shifted over many years, not whether one recent weather event is unusual.
Remember: a place with a snowy climate can have a week without snow, a dry climate can have one rainstorm, and a windy climate can have one calm day — and none of that changes the climate.

problemText: A biome is defined by three main characteristics. Which set of three characteristics do geographers use to identify and name a biome?
choices: Temperature, precipitation, and plant life
Elevation, wind speed, and animal species
Soil type, latitude, and hours of daylight
Humidity, rainfall patterns, and tree height
hints: Think about what the lesson said makes each biome unique and recognizable.
Two of the three characteristics are measurable quantities that describe water and heat.

problemText: A geography class reads this short description: 'Very little water falls here in any month of the year, and the ground between widely spaced plants is mostly bare.' Which biome does this describe, and why is plant life an important clue here?
choices: Tundra, because plant life shows that low temperatures prevent trees from growing in this dry place
Desert, because plant life shows that very little water supports only scattered, spaced-out plants with bare ground between them
Grassland, because plant life shows that moderate rainfall allows grasses to grow across the ground, though they remain spread far apart with visible bare soil between them
Rainforest, because plant life shows that dense trees and shrubs cover nearly all the ground with very little bare space, indicating heavy year-round precipitation
hints: Very low precipitation matches two biomes in the lesson; which plant-life pattern—bare ground or moss-and-shrub coverage—matches this description?
Notice the description says plants are 'spaced far apart' and the ground is 'mostly bare,' not covered by mosses or shrubs.

problemText: A student reads a description of a place where rain falls on most days all year long, with no dry season at all, and the temperature stays hot every month without much change. The student guesses 'forest' as the biome. What is wrong with this guess, and what should the student check before deciding?
choices: The guess ignores the precipitation clue; forests do not receive rain every day all year long, only rainforests do, and daily year-round rain is the signature pattern of a rainforest
The guess ignores the temperature clue; forests can be hot and wet, but a rainforest is always colder than a forest
The guess ignores the plant-life clue; a forest must have a cold season, but this place is hot all year with heavy year-round rain, which points to rainforest instead
The guess ignores the plant-life clue; forests have scattered trees, but this place must have grassland because there is so much rain
hints: A forest needs what temperature pattern that this place does NOT have?
Both forest and rainforest grow many trees; the temperature pattern is what sets them apart.

problemText: A nature preserve in central Africa has a warm season and a cooler season each year. Rainfall is heavy enough to support many trees growing close together throughout the year. Some of the trees lose their leaves during the cool season. A visiting student claims this must be a rainforest. Is the student correct? Explain using all three clues why or why not.
choices: No, the student is wrong. A rainforest is hot all year with no real cool season, but this place has a genuine cool season. A forest, not a rainforest, has both warm and cold seasons and enough rain for many trees, with some trees that lose leaves when cold arrives.

Yes, the student is correct. The presence of heavy rainfall and many trees growing close together are sufficient to classify any location as a rainforest, since these two characteristics define the rainforest biome and override other seasonal variations in temperature.

No, the student is wrong. This place experiences a cool season, and because it also has some trees losing their leaves, it cannot be a rainforest since rainforests maintain constant warm temperatures and trees that retain their leaves year-round.

Yes, the student is correct. While rainforests typically experience warm conditions, the combination of heavy rainfall throughout the year and dense tree growth in this location are the defining features that make it a rainforest despite the presence of a cooler season.
hints: What is the key temperature difference between rainforest (which stays ___ all year) and forest (which has both ___ and ___ seasons)?
Rainforest and forest both have enough rain for many trees; the temperature pattern is what separates them.

problemText: A student is given four short descriptions and asked to match each to the correct biome by checking all three clues. The student correctly matches three of them but makes one error. Description 1: 'Stays cold nearly all year with very little rain and a ground covered by mosses'—student says tundra (correct). Description 2: 'Hot all year, rains on most days, dense trees in layers'—student says rainforest (correct). Description 3: 'Warm part of year, cold part of year, enough rain for many trees, some trees lose leaves in cold'—student says rainforest (WRONG). Description 4: 'Warm season, cooler season, grasses cover most ground, only scattered trees'—student says grassland (correct). For Description 3, which single clue should the student have examined more carefully, and what is the correct biome?
choices: The precipitation clue: rainforest gets year-round heavy rain, but this place gets rain only part of the year, so it is grassland, not rainforest
The temperature clue: rainforest stays hot all year with no cold season, but this place has a genuine cold season, so it is forest, not rainforest
The plant-life clue: rainforest has dense layered trees, but this place has trees that lose leaves, so it must be tundra, not rainforest
The temperature clue: rainforest is warm during one part of the year and cold during another, but this place stays warm all year, so it must be grassland, not rainforest
hints: Rainforest and forest both have enough rain for many trees and both can have trees that lose leaves; what is the one temperature pattern that rainforest requires all year that this description does NOT have?
Re-read what the lesson says rainforest must be like for the whole year, and what forest needs to have happen during the year.
